Microsoft fixes broken Excel copy and paste for all Office users

Microsoft released fixes for an Excel bug caused by September 2026 updates that made copy, paste, autofill, and formula dragging fail silently across several Office versions. Users must manually install the relevant Office updates; Paste Special may temporarily work for Office 2016 and LTSC 2019 workbooks with conditional formatting.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft fixed a known issue caused by September 2026 security updates that could make Excel copy-and-paste operations fail silently.
  • 02The issue affected Excel 2024, 2021, 2019, and 2016, as well as Excel Online in Office Online Server, and also disrupted autofill and formula dragging for some users.
  • 03Affected users must manually download and install the applicable updates for Office 2016, Office LTSC 2019, Office LTSC 2021, or Office LTSC 2024.
  • 04Microsoft warned that copy-and-paste may still fail in Office 2016 and Office LTSC 2019 workbooks containing conditional formatting, for which Paste Special is a temporary workaround.

Microsoft has released fixes for an issue in which Excel copy-and-paste operations could fail silently after September 2026 security updates, including KB5002914. The problem was reported by customers and affected Excel 2016, 2019, 2021, and 2024, as well as Excel Online in Office Online Server. In addition to pasting, users reported problems with autofill and dragging formulas.

Microsoft said users must manually download and install the applicable updates: KB5002665 for Office 2016, Build 10417.20208 for Office LTSC 2019, Build 14334.20918 for Office LTSC 2021, and Build 17932.21000 for Office LTSC 2024. During the failure, copied material remains selected but the destination is not changed, and users receive no error message or sound alert. Microsoft warned that Office 2016 and Office LTSC 2019 may still experience paste failures in workbooks with conditional formatting, for which it recommends Paste Special as a temporary workaround.

  • The Excel failure was silent: copied content remained selected while the destination cell stayed unchanged, with no error message or sound alert to tell users the paste did not occur.
  • The remediation is not described as automatic; users of the affected Office versions need to manually obtain and install version-specific updates.
  • Even after the available fixes, Office 2016 and Office LTSC 2019 may still have paste failures when a workbook contains conditional formatting, making Paste Special the documented temporary option for those cases.

Microsoft fixed a problem caused by September 2026 updates that could make copying and pasting in Excel fail without any warning. It affected people using Excel 2016, 2019, 2021, 2024, and the browser-based version used with Office Online Server, and could also disrupt filling cells or dragging formulas. Users need to manually install the matching Microsoft update, although some older versions may still have problems in files that use special formatting rules.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific Microsoft Office update issue with practical productivity impact, but it does not describe a security vulnerability, active threat activity, breach, or exploitation. Security professionals may only need awareness if they manage Office update deployments.

CISA alerts of active exploitation of three Linux kernel flaws

CISA added three actively exploited Linux kernel vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, including a 14-year-old AF_ALG race condition, and ordered U.S. federal agencies to patch and conduct forensic triage immediately.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities—CVE-2025-39964, CVE-2026-53266, and CVE-2025-39682—to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after reporting they were exploited in attacks.
  • 02CISA gave the vulnerabilities its highest priority for U.S. federal agencies, requiring available patches or mitigations by the end of the day and forensic triage of affected assets.
  • 03CVE-2025-39964 is a 14-year-old race condition in Linux’s AF_ALG cryptographic socket interface that can corrupt per-socket state and may crash systems or alter cryptographic results.
  • 04Public exploits are available for CVE-2025-39682, and Red Hat confirmed known exploit availability for CVE-2026-53266.
  • 05None of the three vulnerabilities is currently flagged as exploited by ransomware groups.

CISA warned that attackers are actively exploiting three Linux kernel vulnerabilities: CVE-2025-39964, CVE-2026-53266, and CVE-2025-39682. The agency assigned them its highest priority for U.S. federal agencies, requiring available updates or mitigations by the end of the day. CISA also designated all three for forensic triage, meaning agencies must check every affected asset for signs of prior exploitation.

CVE-2025-39964 is a 14-year-old race condition in Linux’s AF_ALG cryptographic socket interface that can corrupt per-socket state, potentially crashing systems or changing cryptographic results. STAR Labs demonstrated privilege escalation and container escape using the flaw in Google’s kernelCTF, while public exploits are available for CVE-2025-39682 and Red Hat confirmed a known exploit for CVE-2026-53266. The latter issue may allow changes to shared file-backed memory, although a proposed privilege-escalation chain based on an analogy to Dirty Pipe has not been publicly demonstrated; none of the three flaws is currently flagged as used by ransomware groups.

  • CISA’s “forensic triage” designation means federal agencies must not only patch but also examine every affected asset for evidence that exploitation may already have occurred.
  • CVE-2025-39964 remained in the Linux kernel for 14 years before being identified, and STAR Labs demonstrated privilege escalation and container escape with it in Google’s kernelCTF.
  • Although Red Hat confirms a known exploit for CVE-2026-53266, a researcher’s proposed file-backed-memory privilege-escalation chain has not been publicly demonstrated and is described as inferred from Dirty Pipe by analogy.
  • The reported impacts span more than system crashes: the flaws may alter cryptographic results, modify shared file-backed memory, or cause different TLS record types to be processed together when kernel TLS is used.

The U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA says attackers are actively using three security weaknesses in Linux, the software that powers many computers and servers. One weakness has existed for 14 years, and publicly available attack code exists for two of the issues. U.S. federal agencies were told to install available fixes immediately and check affected systems for signs they may already have been compromised, because the flaws could let attackers crash systems, alter data, or gain higher levels of access.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a must-read alert covering three Linux kernel flaws that CISA says are actively exploited, including one rated critical and one with public exploits available. CISA ordered urgent patching or mitigation and forensic triage for affected U.S. federal assets, signaling potential compromise risk beyond routine patching.

Microsoft reminds admins to migrate Entra ID users to passkeys

Microsoft is urging Entra ID administrators to move users from SMS first-factor sign-in to phishing-resistant options such as passkeys or FIDO2 security keys before SMS sign-in is fully retired on February 1, 2027.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft will retire SMS sign-in as a first-factor authentication method for Entra ID workforce tenants on February 1, 2027.
  • 02Organizations should migrate users to phishing-resistant alternatives such as passkeys, FIDO2 security keys, or QR code authentication to prevent sign-in disruptions.
  • 03The retirement applies even when an organization uses Choose Your Own Telephony Provider for SMS or voice as a multifactor authentication method.
  • 04Microsoft stopped enabling SMS sign-in for newly created Entra ID Free tenants after retiring the feature for existing Free tenants in August.
  • 05Administrators can use Microsoft’s Entra SMS/Voice Policy Scanner PowerShell script to identify users who rely on SMS or voice authentication.

Microsoft is reminding administrators to move Microsoft Entra ID users away from SMS first-factor sign-in before it is retired on February 1, 2027. The change affects Entra ID workforce tenant authentication scenarios and follows Microsoft’s concerns about phishing, fraud, and account compromise risks. SMS and voice will no longer be available as native Microsoft Entra capabilities for sign-in and multifactor authentication after the transition.

Organizations can migrate users to phishing-resistant options including passkeys, FIDO2 security keys, and QR code authentication. The retirement still applies if an organization uses Choose Your Own Telephony Provider for SMS or voice multifactor authentication. Administrators can identify users relying on SMS or voice with Microsoft’s Entra SMS/Voice Policy Scanner PowerShell script, while organizations that must retain phone-based authentication need to configure a third-party telecom provider through the Microsoft Security Store.

  • The change is limited to Microsoft Entra ID workforce tenants and does not apply to Azure AD B2C or Microsoft Entra External ID customer identity scenarios.
  • Using a third-party telephony provider does not preserve SMS sign-in as a first-factor method after the retirement date.
  • As passkeys become the default Entra ID authentication experience, users enabled for SMS or voice will be automatically enabled for passkeys and prompted to register one at their next multifactor authentication.
  • Organizations that still require phone-based authentication must configure a third-party telecom provider through the Microsoft Security Store.

Microsoft says organizations using its Entra ID account service need to stop relying on text messages as the first step for signing in by February 1, 2027. Text-message and phone-call sign-ins are being removed because they can be used in scams, fraud, and account takeovers. Organizations should move affected workers to safer choices such as passkeys, QR-code sign-in, or physical security keys so people do not lose access to their accounts.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a broadly relevant Microsoft Entra ID authentication-policy change that can cause future sign-in disruptions for organizations still using SMS first-factor authentication. Security and identity administrators have substantial lead time, but should identify affected users and plan migration to supported alternatives.

BigCommerce alerts merchants of data breach linked to Ribon apps

BigCommerce removed the compromised Ribon and Ribon 1.5 third-party apps after attackers used stolen app credentials to inject scripts and access customer records at a small number of merchant stores. Exposed data may include names, emails, phone numbers, and shipping addresses, while payment card data and BigCommerce’s core platform were not affected.
KEY POINTS
  • 01BigCommerce said attackers compromised credentials for the third-party Ribon and Ribon 1.5 applications and used them to inject malicious scripts into a small number of merchant storefronts.
  • 02BigCommerce confirmed the credential compromise on September 17 and removed the applications from affected stores to revoke the attackers’ access.
  • 03The attackers accessed shopper data in BigCommerce environments between September 13 and September 17, according to the company.
  • 04Master of Malt said affected shopper information included full names, email addresses, phone numbers, and shipping postal addresses.
  • 05BigCommerce said its platform was not breached and that account passwords and payment card information were stored separately and were not exposed.

BigCommerce notified multiple merchants of a data breach after attackers compromised credentials for the third-party Ribon and Ribon 1.5 applications. The credentials were used between September 13 and September 17 to inject malicious scripts into a small number of merchant storefronts and access shopper data in BigCommerce environments. BigCommerce confirmed the compromise on September 17 and removed the apps from affected stores to revoke the attackers’ access.

UK online spirits retailer Master of Malt said affected information included customers’ full names, email addresses, phone numbers, and shipping postal addresses. BigCommerce said its own platform was not breached, and that account passwords and payment card information were stored separately and were not exposed. Master of Malt reported the matter to the UK Information Commissioner’s Office and said the incident could affect hundreds of stores using the shared Ribon application. Unlike a 2024 incident involving the FreshClick BigCommerce app and ZAGG, this case involved access to existing customer records rather than the capture of payment details at checkout.

  • The incident demonstrates that compromised credentials for a third-party store add-on can expose customer records across multiple merchants without a breach of BigCommerce’s own platform.
  • BigCommerce’s removal of the Ribon applications from affected stores was intended to immediately cut off the attackers’ access, while provided log data could help the app developer investigate.
  • Unlike the 2024 FreshClick incident affecting ZAGG, which captured payment details during checkout, this incident involved access to customer information already stored in BigCommerce environments.
  • Master of Malt said the impact may extend beyond its own customers to potentially hundreds of stores, reflecting the reach of a shared third-party application.

BigCommerce warned some online retailers that criminals used stolen access details for Ribon shopping apps to get into their stores and add harmful code. Customers of affected stores, including UK spirits seller Master of Malt, may have had their names, email addresses, phone numbers, and delivery addresses exposed. Although payment card details and passwords were stored separately and were not exposed, the incident shows how a security failure at a company that supplies store add-ons can put data held by many retailers at risk.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a concrete third-party application credential compromise affecting BigCommerce merchant storefronts and exposing customer personal data, with potential impact across hundreds of stores. It is broadly relevant to organizations relying on SaaS marketplace integrations, although the article does not describe active exploitation beyond the identified incident or a required customer action.

FBI's CJIS v6.1: What Security Teams Need to Know.

FBI CJIS Security Policy v6.1 strengthens requirements for protecting criminal justice information by requiring 256-bit encryption and monthly vulnerability scanning, while maintaining MFA and compromised-password controls. Agencies should align with their state CSA’s audit timeline but begin implementing the newer controls and collecting continuous compliance evidence now.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CJIS Security Policy version 6.1, published June 25, 2026, refines the control-based modernization introduced in version 6.0.
  • 02Version 6.1 raises the required encryption strength for criminal justice information in transit and at rest outside physically secure locations to at least 256 bits.
  • 03CJIS v6.1 changes the required vulnerability-scanning frequency from at least quarterly to at least monthly.
  • 04Priority 1 controls have been sanctionable since October 1, 2024, while Priority 2, 3, and 4 controls remain in zero-cycle status until September 30, 2027.
  • 05The article states that MFA requirements for privileged and non-privileged accounts and password checks against commonly used or compromised passwords have not materially changed between versions 6.0 and 6.1.

The FBI published CJIS Security Policy version 6.1 on June 25, 2026, refining the control-based modernization introduced in version 6.0. The update raises encryption requirements for criminal justice information sent or stored outside physically secure locations to at least 256-bit strength. It also changes vulnerability scanning from at least quarterly to at least monthly.

Version 6.1 does not automatically establish one immediate audit baseline, because state CJIS Systems Agencies may provide separate implementation and assessment guidance. Priority 1 controls have been sanctionable since October 1, 2024, while Priority 2, 3, and 4 controls remain in zero-cycle status until September 30, 2027; Texas is continuing audits against v5.9.5 through March 31, 2027. The article says MFA and password requirements have not materially changed, but agencies increasingly need to show through ongoing evidence that their controls work consistently.

  • Publication of CJIS v6.1 does not automatically create a single immediate audit baseline, because state CJIS Systems Agencies can set their own implementation and assessment guidance; Texas, for example, plans to audit against v5.9.5 through March 31, 2027.
  • The article indicates that CJIS assessment is shifting beyond periodic audit visits toward baseline assessments, quarterly meetings, secure evidence submission, progress reviews, and eventually continuous assessment.
  • MFA was listed among Michigan State Police’s top audit findings even though the identification and authentication requirements did not materially change between CJIS versions 6.0 and 6.1.
  • Agencies are expected not only to deploy controls but also to consistently demonstrate that they work, making evidence collection a central compliance concern.
  • Waiting until a control becomes sanctionable can create unnecessary later work, particularly as assessment programs move toward more frequent verification.

The FBI updated its rules for organizations that handle criminal justice information, requiring stronger encryption when data is stored or sent outside secure locations and monthly checks for missing security updates. Police agencies and their technology partners are affected, although states may use different timelines for checking compliance. The changes matter because they aim to reduce the risk of unauthorized access to sensitive law-enforcement information by requiring stronger sign-in protections, safer passwords, and proof that security measures continue to work.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

The article covers a concrete CJIS policy update with actionable changes to encryption strength and vulnerability-scanning frequency for organizations handling criminal justice information. However, it is sponsored vendor content and primarily presents compliance guidance rather than an urgent incident, active threat, or critical patch.

Microsoft: September updates break File History backup feature

Microsoft says September 2026 Windows security updates can break File History, preventing backups from being created or updated and triggering misleading drive-reconnection warnings on affected Windows 10 and Windows 11 systems.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft warned that September 2026 Windows security updates may prevent File History from creating or updating backups on some systems.
  • 02Affected users may see FileHistory.exe and KERNELBASE.dll crash events, incorrect “Reconnect your drive” messages, unchanged “Last Backup” timestamps, and unavailable previous file versions.
  • 03Affected releases include Windows 10 21H2 and later, Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2016 and 2019, and Windows 11 23H2 and later.
  • 04The affected updates include KB5124012, KB5124008, KB5122880, KB5122878, KB5122876, and KB5123099.
  • 05Microsoft has also linked the September 2026 updates to Remote Desktop Services, Hyper-V, USB audio, and domain-login issues, with some fixes and workarounds already released.

Microsoft warned that September 2026 Windows security updates can prevent the built-in File History feature from creating or updating backups on some devices. File History saves copies of files from user folders so they can be restored after accidental deletion or damage. Microsoft said affected users may see FileHistory.exe and KERNELBASE.dll crash events in Event Viewer.

Affected systems can also incorrectly display a “Reconnect your drive” message even when a compatible backup drive is connected and working. Other signs include an unchanged “Last Backup” time and previously backed-up files reporting that no earlier version is available. The issue affects Windows 10 21H2 and later, Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2016 and 2019, and Windows 11 23H2 and later, following several listed September cumulative updates.

  • The File History failure can look like a disconnected backup drive even when the drive is connected and functioning properly, which may lead users to misidentify the cause.
  • The issue affects both new backup activity and access to older versions of files, reducing the ability to recover files that were accidentally deleted or damaged.
  • Application crash entries referring to FileHistory.exe and KERNELBASE.dll provide a specific indicator that the backup problem may be related to the September updates.
  • Microsoft’s emergency updates for other September-update problems did not resolve every USB audio issue, while the File History issue remains separately identified in a service alert.

Microsoft says its September 2026 Windows updates can stop the File History feature from making or refreshing copies of personal files. The problem affects some people and organizations using Windows 10 or Windows 11, including long-term support editions, and may falsely tell them to reconnect a backup drive that is already working. This matters because File History helps people restore files that were deleted or damaged, so affected users may not have current copies available when they need them.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a concrete, vendor-confirmed issue affecting Windows backup functionality across multiple Windows 10 and Windows 11 releases. Security professionals responsible for endpoint reliability and recoverability should be aware because the bug can prevent current backups and access to previous file versions, but it is not an active security compromise or critical vulnerability.

WordPress Click2Shell flaw lets hackers execute PHP on the server

WordPress 7.1.0 and earlier contain the Click2Shell CSRF flaw, which can let an attacker trick a logged-in administrator into installing a vulnerable theme and executing arbitrary PHP on the server. Administrators should update to WordPress 7.1.1 immediately.
KEY POINTS
  • 01WordPress 7.1.0 and earlier are affected by the Click2Shell cross-site request forgery flaw, which was fixed in WordPress 7.1.1.
  • 02The flaw can allow an unauthenticated attacker to trick a logged-in WordPress administrator into installing a theme and executing arbitrary PHP code on the server.
  • 03The attack chain relies on a crafted link and can execute PHP from an inactive theme while its Customizer preview loads.
  • 04Successful exploitation could allow file changes or deletion, access to user data and wp-config.php, creation of rogue administrator accounts, and injection of malicious scripts.
  • 05Patchstack said sites with DISALLOW_FILE_MODS enabled cannot be forced to install the theme or a malicious plugin, but recommends updating WordPress.

Technical details and a proof-of-concept exploit have been released for Click2Shell, a cross-site request forgery flaw in WordPress Core 7.1.0 and earlier. The issue was fixed in WordPress 7.1.1, released last week. It allows an unauthenticated attacker to use a crafted link to make a logged-in administrator install a theme from the official WordPress.org catalog and execute arbitrary PHP on the server.

The attack exploits a theme-preview value that is handled differently by the WordPress.org Themes API and JavaScript in the administrator’s browser. Although the installed theme can be inactive, its PHP can execute when its Customizer preview loads. Successful attacks could allow file changes or deletion, access to user data and wp-config.php, rogue administrator-account creation, or malicious script injection. Patchstack noted that DISALLOW_FILE_MODS prevents forced theme or plugin installation, but updating to WordPress 7.1.1 is strongly recommended.

  • The exploit chain does not require the attacker to have a WordPress account, an installation nonce, or administrator privileges; it only requires a logged-in administrator to open a crafted link.
  • Even an inactive theme can run PHP code when WordPress loads it in the Customizer preview, allowing a forced-installed vulnerable theme to become part of the code-execution chain.
  • The underlying WordPress Core issue could force-install any vulnerable theme available in the official WordPress.org catalog, not only the theme used in the demonstration.
  • Enabling DISALLOW_FILE_MODS prevents the forced installation of the theme or a malicious plugin for sites that cannot immediately update.

A flaw called Click2Shell in WordPress 7.1.0 and older can let someone send a special link to a logged-in site administrator and, if the administrator opens it, add a harmful website theme and run code on the site’s server. This affects WordPress websites whose administrators could be tricked into visiting such a link. An intruder could then change or delete files, view user and database information, create unauthorized administrator accounts, or add harmful content. WordPress fixed the issue in version 7.1.1, so site owners should update.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a broadly relevant WordPress Core flaw with public technical details and a proof-of-concept that can lead to server-side code execution when a logged-in administrator visits a crafted link. Security professionals responsible for WordPress sites should prioritize updating to version 7.1.1.

Microsoft to retire Microsoft 365 Companion apps in December

Microsoft will retire its Windows 11 taskbar-integrated Microsoft 365 Calendar, People, and Files companion apps on December 16, 2026; they will no longer function or receive support. The company has stopped automatically installing them and advises administrators to remove them from managed devices before the deadline.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft will retire the Microsoft 365 Calendar, People, and Files companion apps on December 16, 2026, after which they will no longer function or be supported.
  • 02The companion apps were designed to integrate with the Windows 11 taskbar, helping users access schedules, contacts, Microsoft 365 files, and locally stored files.
  • 03Microsoft has stopped installing the companion apps through Microsoft 365 Apps updates as of Friday.
  • 04Microsoft advises administrators to remove the companion apps from devices in their organization before the December 2026 retirement date.
  • 05Users of unmanaged devices have also been asked to uninstall the companion apps themselves.

Microsoft will retire its Microsoft 365 companion apps—Calendar, People, and Files—on December 16, 2026. After that date, the apps will no longer function or receive support. Microsoft advises administrators to remove them from devices in their organization before the retirement deadline.

The taskbar-integrated Windows 11 apps were designed to help users check schedules, look up contacts, and access Microsoft 365 and locally stored files, with Copilot providing contextual assistance. Once installed, they launched automatically at startup by default, although administrators could opt out of automatic installation and users could disable auto-launch in each app’s settings. Microsoft has stopped installing the apps through Microsoft 365 Apps updates and has asked users of unmanaged devices to uninstall them themselves.

  • The companion apps were set to launch automatically at sign-in by default, so organizations may have them present on compatible Windows 11 devices even if users did not explicitly install or open them.

  • 01A fake LastPass Authenticator page on GitHub directed visitors to a ZIP file containing a malicious installer, while the legitimate app is available only through lastpass.com and official app stores.
  • 02The installer used DLL side-loading with a renamed Microsoft debugging tool to gain administrator-level access and install the Microsoft-signed Alinubx.sys kernel driver.

A fake LastPass Authenticator download page on GitHub led victims through several pages to a large ZIP archive hosted on an attacker-controlled server. The archive contained a malicious installer that used a renamed Microsoft debugging tool and a malicious DLL to load attacker code. LastPass said its own systems, services, and customer vaults were not affected, as the attackers only impersonated its brand. The real LastPass Authenticator is distributed through lastpass.com and official app stores, not GitHub.

The installer gained elevated access, installed the Microsoft-signed Alinubx.sys kernel driver, and used it to terminate antivirus and other security processes from below the level where those tools run. The driver was a renamed copy of CcProtect.sys from the Chinese disk-encryption product CnCrypt, was not on Microsoft’s vulnerable-driver blocklist, and had zero VirusTotal detections when researchers checked it in August. With security software disabled, the Rapuncel stealer collected browser passwords, cryptocurrency wallet files, Discord, Steam, and Telegram sessions, Windows Credential Manager data, and files with names such as “password,” “seed,” or “recovery.” The article advises anyone who ran the payload to treat the machine as a kernel-level compromise, change affected passwords from a clean device, and, where possible, rebuild the machine or conduct a kernel-level forensic check.

  • A Microsoft hardware-compatibility signature did not prevent abuse: the driver had zero VirusTotal detections in August and was not on Microsoft's blocklist despite being able to terminate security software.
  • The attackers padded the ZIP archives to 127.9 MB and 148 MB with junk files, apparently to evade scanners that skip large files because of size limits.
  • The stealer bypassed Chrome and Edge's app-bound encryption by injecting code into the browsers and using the browsers' own services to decrypt saved passwords.
  • Defenders are advised to hunt for the driver's signing lineage and behavior, such as the NvFsFilter service and security-process termination, because file-name or hash-only detections can be defeated when the driver is renamed or changed.

Criminals created a fake LastPass Authenticator download page on GitHub that can install software designed to turn off a computer’s security protections and steal saved passwords, cryptocurrency wallet files, and account sign-ins. People who downloaded and ran it are affected, while LastPass says its own systems and customer password vaults were not touched. This matters because the harmful program uses a driver that Windows trusted, showing that a familiar brand name and a trusted-looking download can still lead to a serious computer takeover.

Researchers at Securonix disclosed TASK#STOMP, a PowerShell backdoor that steals business documents, Wi-Fi passwords, clipboard contents, system information, and screenshots from compromised Windows systems. It also monitors the filesystem for new or modified files and can run arbitrary PowerShell commands received from its command-and-control servers. The malware is designed to maintain long-term access while collecting sensitive data.

The infection chain begins when wscript.exe runs an encoded VBScript file with a random filename on the victim’s desktop. That script creates scheduled tasks with legitimate-sounding names and adds a Startup-folder script as a backup way to run whenever the user logs in. Two hidden PowerShell components use separate but shared command-and-control infrastructure, monitor and restart one another, and use built-in Windows components, hidden execution, timestamp changes, and cleanup behavior to make detection and forensic review more difficult.

  • The scheduled tasks are given names resembling legitimate Windows services, such as Local Credential Manager and Windows Display Manager, which can make them less conspicuous during routine review.
  • The campaign relies largely on built-in Windows components and dynamically compiled C# code rather than conventional executable payloads, making individual malicious events harder to distinguish from normal administrative activity.

Researchers found a new malicious program called TASK#STOMP that can secretly collect business documents, saved Wi-Fi passwords, copied text, and screen images from infected Windows computers. It can also let attackers run commands remotely and keep returning even if part of the program is removed. The first way computers are infected is not known, but the activity may begin with a deceptive email or social-engineering trick. This matters because the attackers can quietly steal sensitive information and maintain long-term access while making their activity look like normal Windows behavior.

A Carrier-Registry Phish With a Browser's CSS Pasted In

A phishing email impersonating the U.S. Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and link scans because it used attacker-owned infrastructure, but its HTML exposed browser-derived markdown styling residue from copy-pasted content. Hunting for such foreign renderer artifacts in inbound email can provide a useful additional signal for detecting polished phishing lures seeking carrier identity and payment information.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A phishing email impersonating the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration asked recipients to confirm carrier identity, DOT, fuel-tax, and payment-system information through a lookalike registry portal.
  • 02The attacker-owned sending domain passed SPF, two DKIM signatures, DMARC alignment, and URL scanning, while having no prior bad history at the recipient tenant.
  • 03Thirteen paragraphs in the email HTML contained browser-style residue, including the ds-markdown-paragraph class, quote-cjk-patch font, and inert print-layout properties such as orphans and widows.
  • 04The recipient organization was a facilities and building-services company with no carrier authority, and the greeting named an unrelated company, indicating a badly targeted bulk merge.
  • 05The recipient platform routed the message to junk as bulk spam and quarantined the mailbox within three minutes, after which a human analyst classified the incident as malicious.

A commercial facilities and property-services company received an email impersonating the U.S. Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration and asking it to confirm carrier details through a lookalike registry portal. The message sought motor-carrier and DOT numbers, legal business information, and fuel-tax and payment-system details, rather than passwords. The recipient was not a carrier and had no carrier authority, while the greeting named an unrelated company, indicating that the bulk merge was poorly targeted.

The attacker-owned domain passed SPF, two DKIM signatures, DMARC alignment, and URL scanning, so those checks confirmed the attacker’s configured infrastructure rather than the message’s legitimacy. However, thirteen HTML paragraphs contained browser-derived styling residue, including ds-markdown-paragraph, quote-cjk-patch, and print-layout properties such as orphans and widows, suggesting text was copied from a browser into a separate email template. The recipient platform routed the email to junk as bulk spam and quarantined the mailbox within three minutes, but the article argues that searching inbound HTML for foreign renderer artifacts can provide an additional detection signal for similar lures.

  • Passing email-authentication checks did not establish legitimacy in this case; it verified that the attacker-controlled domain and its message were configured correctly.
  • The email preserved a visible boundary between the attacker’s sending template and text pasted from a browser, allowing the composing environment to be distinguished from the infrastructure used to deliver the message.
  • Browser-derived HTML features such as print-layout settings, unusual font names, and foreign renderer class names can be used as weighted content signals when combined with factors such as first contact and the requested information.
  • The message was stopped as bulk spam rather than because its deception was identified directly, making the protection dependent on sending behavior that an attacker can change.
  • A functional one-click unsubscribe link supplied by the sending platform made the bulk fraud resemble ordinary marketing email.

A fake email claiming to be from the U.S. Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration asked recipients to confirm trucking-company details and fuel-tax payment information through a lookalike website. Although the message appeared legitimate in many automated checks, it contained hidden clues showing that text had been copied from a browser-based writing tool and pasted into the scammer’s email template. The recipient company was not even a carrier, suggesting the scam was sent broadly, but real trucking businesses could lose sensitive company and payment information that may enable freight fraud or redirected payments.

This is a concrete phishing incident with a useful technical finding: browser-derived HTML residue exposed the attacker’s copy-and-paste composition process despite clean authentication and link-scanning results. It is most relevant to email-security analysts and defenders hunting phishing content, but describes a single narrowly targeted campaign rather than a broadly urgent event.

Aikido introduced Altar, its first open-weight security model, intended to provide advanced AI capabilities within customer-controlled infrastructure, including air-gapped environments. The model is designed to support Aikido Machine, an autonomous pentesting appliance that can detect, exploit, and validate vulnerabilities without sending sensitive organizational context to third-party inference services. Aikido positions this as important for organizations such as banks, hospital groups, and industrial operators that face data-residency, data-processing, or connectivity constraints. Altar is also intended for Aikido Attack, Code Security Audit, and Deep PR Review workflows.

Altar was built from GLM-5.3 using AWQ INT4 quantization and expert pruning with Cerebras REAP. It retains 168 of 256 routed experts in each backbone expert layer, reducing stored weights from 1,506.7 GB for full-precision GLM-5.3 and 488.2 GB for its unpruned AWQ version to 328.0 GB. On Aikido’s internal CVE benchmark, Altar averaged 60.4% recall per run and rediscovered 23 of 32 known vulnerabilities across three runs, compared with 61.5% recall and the same coverage for quantized GLM-5.3. Aikido says Altar can be served with the latest vLLM on a node with four NVIDIA H200 GPUs and that it identified a valid critical-severity vulnerability during a client production pentest after deployment.

  • Pruning experts based on security-testing traces alone could weaken language understanding, so Aikido added multilingual text to preserve the ability to interpret application documentation and business rules in languages such as French and Dutch.
  • Models with the same number of retained experts can differ substantially in how closely they match the original model, meaning the selection method is as important as the amount of compression.
  • Altar’s reduction from the 488.2 GB quantized parent to 328.0 GB resulted in about one percentage point lower average recall while preserving the same 23-of-32 vulnerability coverage across three runs.
  • The article distinguishes between finding a known flaw at least once and finding it reliably: its coverage metric measures whether a vulnerability was found across three runs, while average recall reflects consistency per run.

Aikido released Altar, a smaller version of an AI system designed to help find security weaknesses in software and computer systems while running entirely inside an organization’s own environment. This matters to banks, hospitals, industrial operators, and other groups that cannot send sensitive code, internal documents, or security findings to outside AI services. Aikido says the model keeps most of its ability to identify known software flaws despite requiring far less storage, making private, locally run AI security testing more practical.

SAML: A fractal of bad design

The article argues that SAML should be retired in favor of OpenID Connect because its XML-based design, canonicalization and enveloped-signature complexity, and decades of accumulated features make secure implementations unusually difficult. Organizations should favor OIDC for new SSO integrations and plan gradual migrations away from existing SAML deployments.
KEY POINTS
  • 01SAML was created in 2002 and became a foundation for the single sign-on industry as organizations needed a way to authenticate users to many web services.
  • 02The article identifies XML signature wrapping, XML canonicalization, enveloped signatures, kitchen-sink design, and protocol ossification as major long-term flaws in SAML.
  • 03XML signature wrapping attacks against SAML have been studied for years and remain present in modern implementations, according to the article.
  • 04The author argues that XML’s complexity and security bug classes make securely implementing SAML more difficult than using simpler JSON-based alternatives.
  • 05The article recommends OpenID Connect for new single sign-on integrations and proposes that identity providers gradually migrate existing SAML customers to equivalent OpenID Connect configurations.

The article argues that Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML), created in 2002, should be deprecated in favor of OpenID Connect (OIDC). SAML helped establish the single sign-on industry by allowing organizations to authenticate users across many web services, and it was adopted by academic projects, corporate identity systems, and providers such as Ping Identity, OneLogin, Okta, and Duo Security. Despite that history, the author says SAML is now burdened by complexity and recurring security weaknesses.

A central concern is XML signature wrapping, along with XML canonicalization, enveloped signatures, parser differences, and XML-specific bug classes such as external entity processing and entity expansion. The article says that modern SAML attacks still exploit round-trip and parser-differential behavior, even though signature-wrapping issues have been researched for years. It also criticizes SAML’s broad, largely unused feature set and its design assumptions from an earlier era of disconnected corporate networks.

The author presents OIDC as a more suitable modern alternative because it uses simpler JSON-based formats, commonly relies on HTTPS and direct communication between participating services, and has evolved through focused specifications for changing needs. Service providers are encouraged to support OIDC rather than add SAML, while identity providers are encouraged to stop onboarding new SAML integrations, offer equivalent OIDC configurations, communicate a deprecation plan, and set a sunset date. The article concludes that SAML made major contributions to authentication and single sign-on but should be replaced through gradual migration.

  • The article notes that most modern SAML deployments use a similar narrow subset of the specification, meaning they carry complexity from many seldom-used features without benefiting from them.
  • SAML’s original ability to work when the identity provider and service provider could not communicate directly was useful in older corporate network environments, but the article says OpenID Connect’s form-post flow can provide the same ingredients.
  • Direct communication between an OpenID Connect identity provider and relying service can move information exchange to a backchannel, reducing the amount of data and complexity required in the authentication response.
  • For organizations still supporting SAML, the article presents a practical migration sequence: stop adding new SAML customers, provide equivalent OpenID Connect setups, announce a sunset date, and transition existing customers over time.

The article argues that SAML, an older system used to let employees sign in once and access many workplace web services, has become too complicated to use safely. Its underlying data format and signing rules have repeatedly led to mistakes that can let attackers impersonate users, affecting companies, schools, identity-service providers, and the services that rely on them. The author says newer options such as OpenID Connect are simpler and better suited to modern web, mobile, and connected-device use, so organizations should gradually move away from SAML.

Group Policy hijacked: PAYLOAD ransomware weaponizes Active Directory GPO

Kaspersky investigated a Middle Eastern manufacturer where attackers with domain-level Active Directory control used malicious, domain-root-linked GPOs to deploy ransom notes, replace wallpapers and lock screens, disable local administrator accounts, and turn off Windows Firewall without encrypting Windows data or deploying endpoint malware. The case shows that GPO abuse can enable stealthy, domain-wide encryptionless extortion, making AD change auditing and SYSVOL monitoring critical defenses.
KEY POINTS
  • 01In April 2026, Kaspersky investigated an incident at a Middle Eastern manufacturing organization in which an attacker used a compromised domain account to access the network through FortiGate SSL VPN.
  • 02The attacker created and linked a malicious domain-root Group Policy Object named PAYLOAD that distributed ransom notes, changed desktop wallpaper and lock screens, displayed a ransom banner at sign-in, and disabled the local Administrator account on domain-joined Windows systems.
  • 03A second domain-root Group Policy Object named "win Firewall Off" disabled Windows Firewall across domain, private, and public profiles on endpoints.
  • 04The visible effects began a day after the malicious policies were created because the affected computers applied the computer settings when they rebooted.
  • 05Kaspersky found no Windows file encryption, resident endpoint malware, endpoint persistence, or active malicious processes, although data exfiltration from file servers and other systems was observed and later published on the dark web.

In April 2026, Kaspersky investigated an incident at a manufacturing organization in the Middle East where an attacker used a compromised domain account to access the network through FortiGate SSL VPN. The attacker obtained domain administrator-equivalent control and created a malicious Group Policy Object (GPO) named PAYLOAD, linking it at the Active Directory domain root. The GPO distributed ransom notes, replaced desktop wallpaper and lock-screen images, enforced a logon banner, and disabled the local Administrator account across domain-joined Windows systems. A second GPO, named “win Firewall Off,” disabled Windows Firewall across all endpoint profiles.

The attackers staged a ransom image and text file in the domain controller’s SYSVOL share, then used the trusted Windows policy system to distribute them. Visible disruption began the following day as endpoints rebooted and applied the computer policy settings, while data exfiltration from file servers and other systems was observed and later published on the dark web. Kaspersky found no Windows file encryption, resident endpoint malware, malicious processes, or conventional endpoint persistence; the GPO links and policy files were the persistence mechanism. The incident demonstrates that attackers with high-level Active Directory control can cause domain-wide disruption and extort an organization without deploying a ransomware binary to Windows endpoints.

The article recommends prioritizing removal of the malicious GPOs and SYSVOL artifacts on domain controllers before cleaning endpoints, because policy refreshes can reapply the malicious settings. It also recommends auditing Active Directory changes, especially GPO creation and modifications to domain-root policy links, and monitoring SYSVOL for suspicious files or changes. Additional hardening measures include phishing-resistant MFA for remote access, credential rotation, tiered administration, Windows LAPS, Credential Guard, privileged access workstations, and centralized FortiGate logging. Kaspersky emphasizes that file- and process-based detection alone may not identify this attack class, making directory-service auditing and SYSVOL integrity monitoring important controls.

  • The malicious activity was stored in Active Directory and its shared policy files rather than in a ransomware program on employee computers, so cleaning individual computers would not remove the source of the disruption.
  • The one-day delay between policy creation and visible impact gave the attackers time to exfiltrate data and made it harder to connect the later disruption to the earlier directory changes.
  • The use of user-policy loopback processing ensured that the ransom wallpaper applied regardless of which user signed in to an affected computer.
  • A change to the domain-root policy link by an unusual account is a particularly strong detection signal because it can apply a policy across the entire domain.
  • Unexpected changes in the shared policy-file location without matching directory-change records can indicate direct editing of policy files, although incomplete audit configuration can also cause missing records.

Attackers broke into a manufacturing company in the Middle East using a stolen account and took control of the company’s central Windows management system. They used it to put ransom messages and images on employees’ computers, disable a local administrator account, and turn off built-in firewalls across the organization, even though they did not encrypt files on Windows machines. This matters because criminals can disrupt an entire company and pressure it to pay without installing obvious harmful software, while also stealing data that may later be published online.

La majorité du trafic internet n’est pas humaine: comprendre les bots

A significant share of internet traffic is automated, with bots used both for legitimate tasks and for fraud such as credential stuffing, fake-account creation, scraping, and scalping. Defending against them requires continuously combining browser, network, and behavioral signals, because CAPTCHAs, IP blocks, and single detection methods can all be bypassed at scale.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Bots are programs that automate actions on the internet and can operate continuously, much faster than people, and at very large scale.
  • 02Bots can support legitimate uses such as search indexing, automated testing, and service monitoring, but they are also used for credential stuffing, fake-account creation, payment-card testing, scraping, and scalping.
  • 03Websites detect suspected bots by combining signals from browser characteristics, network addresses, user interactions, action history, and request frequency rather than relying on a single test.
  • 04Attackers can make automated traffic appear more legitimate by altering browser characteristics, solving CAPTCHAs through services, and rotating requests through large proxy networks.
  • 05Bot defense has no perfect solution because aggressive blocking can prevent legitimate users from accessing services, while bots continually adapt to detection methods.

A significant portion of internet traffic is generated by bots: programs that automate actions such as browsing pages, filling forms, and making requests at far greater speed and scale than a person. Some bots are useful for search indexing, automated testing, and monitoring, while others support credential stuffing, fake-account creation, payment-card testing, scraping, and scalping. The growing availability of graphical tools and shared configurations has lowered the technical barrier to using automated traffic.

Websites attempt to distinguish bots from legitimate users by combining browser characteristics, interaction patterns, network information, and historical context. CAPTCHAs and IP-based blocking are limited because CAPTCHA-solving services, altered browser fingerprints, and large proxy networks can help attackers evade them. Residential proxies are particularly difficult to handle because they use IP addresses that resemble normal consumer connections; the article reports observing around 45 million unique IP addresses in such networks over 30 days. The aim of bot defenses is therefore not perfect detection, but making abuse more costly and harder to scale without unnecessarily blocking real users.

  • CAPTCHAs often function as an operational cost rather than a hard barrier for attackers, with the article citing an automated solving service priced at roughly €0.68 for 1,000 CAPTCHAs.
  • Residential proxy networks can use ordinary consumers’ internet connections through infected devices, questionable mobile apps, or browser extensions, meaning users may unknowingly carry automated traffic.
  • The article reports observing roughly 45 million unique IP addresses used by residential proxy networks over 30 days, illustrating why blocking individual IP addresses does not scale.
  • Attackers can collect and reuse real browser fingerprints in “fingerprint farms,” making automated traffic more credible than traffic from a default automated browser.
  • The article notes that no-code graphical tools and easily shared configurations can enable people to use automation without understanding the targeted site in detail.

The article explains that much of the activity on websites comes from automated programs, not people. Some are useful, such as search-engine programs, but others can rapidly try stolen passwords, create fake accounts, buy scarce tickets or sneakers, and collect website data. This affects online shoppers, account holders, and the websites they use, which often add frustrating checks such as CAPTCHAs, text-message confirmations, and virtual queues to slow abuse. There is no permanent fix because attackers can hide behind many ordinary home internet connections and continually adapt, so services must balance stopping abuse with not blocking real users.

The article examines how AWS responds when an IAM access key and secret are publicly exposed, including in public GitHub repositories. AWS can automatically attach the AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine managed policy to the affected IAM user, which explicitly denies selected high-risk actions. The policy is intended to reduce fraud-related activity and unauthorized charges without fully disabling the user or disrupting all existing resources.

In a public GitHub exposure test, AWS attached AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3 within 10 seconds of the credentials being pushed, followed by a GitHub notification, an AWS Health alert, email, and an AWS Support case. The policy attachment appears in CloudTrail as an IAM AttachUserPolicy event, although the log may name the affected IAM user as the actor even when that user did not perform the action.   • The CloudTrail AttachUserPolicy event created by AWS’s automated quarantine process may identify the affected IAM user as the actor even though that user did not attach the policy, so investigators should avoid treating that field as proof of user action.
  • AWS intentionally uses a targeted deny list instead of disabling the compromised key or user entirely, reducing operational disruption but leaving actions not explicitly denied potentially available to an advanced attacker.
  • AWS Health alerts and Support-case creation for an exposed key did not generate CloudTrail events in the article’s test, making the managed-policy attachment the more useful logging signal for automated detection.
  • GitHub’s secret-validation check produces an AWS STS GetCallerIdentity event in CloudTrail, allowing organizations to detect a likely GitHub-discovered exposure even before relying on email notifications.
  • GitHub push protection can miss secrets in very large pushes or limit alerts when a single push contains more than five exposed secrets, creating cases where additional scanning may be necessary.

The article explains what Amazon Web Services does when an organization accidentally publishes a cloud account key, such as by placing it in a public GitHub code repository. AWS can quickly add a protective restriction to the affected account user, blocking many costly or damaging actions while allowing some normal work to continue, and it sends alerts through GitHub, email, and AWS support tools. This matters to organizations using AWS because stolen keys can let criminals create expensive computing resources, steal or delete stored data, or misuse newer AI services. The article recommends watching AWS activity records and GitHub alerts so security teams can find exposed keys and respond quickly.

Cloud Threat Emulation on Autopilot: Context is Everything

Effective cloud threat emulation is not simply executing attack APIs: it requires realistic threat and victim models, constrained IAM progression, controlled disposable labs, and verification of real telemetry. Teams should evaluate detections against observed events, document assumptions and failures, and rigorously clean up every run.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Cloud threat emulation should follow a plan-first lifecycle that defines objectives and scope, models the threat and victim environment, executes in a controlled lab, verifies telemetry, evaluates coverage, documents findings, and cleans up.
  • 02Cloud emulations should begin from a believable compromised identity with only the permissions available at that stage, rather than using an administrator session that makes the scenario unrealistic.
  • 03Teams should verify actual raw log events and confirm required logging is enabled, because cloud data-access telemetry may be late, partial, absent, or disabled.
  • 04Detection coverage should be evaluated against the events generated by the exercise, since ATT&CK mappings and rules that fire do not necessarily prove that the intended behavior was detected for the right reason.
  • 05Labs should be disposable and use unique run tags, while cleanup must remove both infrastructure created through provisioning tools and attacker-created resources that are not recorded in infrastructure state.

Cloud threat emulation for detection engineering requires more than issuing an API call or running a tool. The article presents a plan-first lifecycle: define the objective and scope, research and model the threat, model the victim environment and initial identity access, build a flow, provision a controlled lab, execute, verify telemetry, evaluate detection coverage, document findings, and clean up. It distinguishes atomic tests, micro emulations, and full emulations, while arguing that the same lifecycle applies at different levels of depth.

Realistic cloud emulation should start from a believable compromised identity and preserve the permissions, dependencies, denials, and adjustments that a real operator would encounter. Teams should confirm logging is enabled and inspect raw events rather than relying on remembered field names, because data may be delayed, incomplete, absent, or not captured by default. The article also recommends disposable, tagged environments, tracking attacker-created resources outside infrastructure-as-code state, and verifying cleanup so labs do not contaminate later tests or leave costly or exposed resources behind.

  • A unique emulation tag is useful for telemetry filtering only when it appears in an identity ARN, such as a user name, role name, or temporary session name; tagging a resource alone does not make it visible in that filter.
  • Cloud data-access activity may not be captured by default: the article notes that AWS CloudTrail management events alone would miss the Amazon S3 GetObject activity needed to make an exfiltration scenario visible.
  • A denied permission request can be valuable detection evidence, because realistic adversaries encounter blocked actions and adapt rather than silently receiving administrator permissions.
  • Cleanup must account for attacker-created users, keys, roles, topics, and grants before destroying provisioned infrastructure, because those artifacts are not necessarily tracked in infrastructure-as-code state.
  • Fixed wait times such as "sleep 30" can make cloud emulations unreliable due to IAM propagation and log delays; polling for readiness and allowing logs to settle is more reliable.

The article explains how organizations can safely copy the steps a real intruder might take in cloud services so they can see whether their security monitoring notices them. It says these exercises need realistic user accounts, permissions, resources, and logging—not just a quick test from an all-powerful administrator account. This matters to companies using cloud services because poor tests can create misleading alerts, miss real warning signs, leave expensive or exposed test resources behind, and result in security tools that fail when a genuine attacker acts.

Vidar Adds Virtual Machine and Custom Stream Ciphers For String Obfuscation

Vidar stealer has evolved its string obfuscation from simple XOR and modified ChaCha20 to per-build virtual-machine bytecode and custom stream ciphers, making static detection and automated analysis substantially harder.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Vidar is an information stealer first observed in 2018 whose string obfuscation evolved from single-byte XOR to ChaCha20-based methods and then to a custom virtual machine and stream cipher.
  • 02From May through early September 2026, Zscaler ThreatLabz observed Vidar using a lightweight bytecode interpreter with per-build-changing opcodes, constants, substitution tables, and a hardcoded XOR key.
  • 03Vidar’s virtual machine can either directly produce a decrypted string or decrypt a key and nonce used by a separate custom stream cipher to decrypt the final string.
  • 04Vidar versions 2.0 and 2.1 used a modified ChaCha-based cipher, while version 2.2 and later used a custom add-rotate-XOR stream cipher with per-build constants and transformations.
  • 05Zscaler lists detections for Vidar under the threat name Win32.PWS.Vidar and provides indicators for versions 2.0, 2.5, 3.1, and 3.4.

Zscaler ThreatLabz analyzed the evolution of Vidar, an information stealer first observed in 2018, from May through early September 2026. Vidar’s developers moved from single-byte XOR string hiding to ChaCha20-based methods and then to a custom virtual machine (VM) combined with custom stream ciphers. These changes are intended to make detection and analysis more difficult by altering algorithms, constants, and low-level operations between builds.

In Vidar versions 2.x and 3.x, a lightweight bytecode interpreter processes VM instructions using a one-byte accumulator and 14 opcode handlers. The VM can either decode a string directly or recover a key and nonce that decrypt a separately encrypted string. Versions 2.0 and 2.1 used a modified ChaCha-based cipher, while version 2.2 and later used a custom add-rotate-XOR cipher with per-build constants and transformations. Zscaler states that its platform detects Vidar-related indicators under the name Win32.PWS.Vidar and provides indicators for versions 2.0, 2.5, 3.1, and 3.4.

  • Vidar’s obfuscation changes its constants, opcode mappings, substitution tables, and cipher operations across builds while preserving the same general interfaces, specifically undermining static signatures that rely on fixed implementation details.
  • The virtual machine is deliberately lightweight, using only a one-byte accumulator and 14 populated opcode handlers in a sparse 256-entry table, yet it can either decode strings directly or recover the key and nonce for a second decryption stage.
  • The four-byte hardcoded XOR key serves two roles in the VM: it seeds the accumulator and is also used during bytecode execution, with its value changing for each build.
  • Beginning with version 2.2, Vidar’s custom stream cipher derives its state from VM-recovered key and nonce material, then applies per-build add-rotate-XOR transformations and constants to generate the byte-by-byte decryption stream.

Vidar is a program that steals information, and its developers have changed how it hides the text and instructions inside the program so security tools and researchers have a harder time finding them. Newer versions use a small built-in instruction reader and a different secret-scrambling method in each copy, rather than relying on one consistent hiding method. This matters because Vidar can target data from web browsers, digital wallets, browser add-ons, and other collected information, while its changing design makes it harder to detect before it can steal that data.

  • 02Technology friction creates a double cost because employees are interrupted and IT staff must spend time resolving issues.
  • 03Common sources of friction include delayed device readiness, login and permission problems, slow devices, storage issues, disruptive updates, and routine requests that require IT intervention.
  • 04Proactive practices such as centralized access, device-health visibility, automated patching and configuration, and self-service workflows can reduce IT overhead and employee disruption.
  • 05Digital Employee Experience (DEX) measures how employees interact with devices, applications, and services so IT can identify and address recurring friction patterns.

Everyday technology friction—such as slow application loading, device restarts, login problems, permission gaps, and software that is not ready when needed—can create substantial productivity loss when experienced across an organization. Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index is cited as finding that employees are interrupted an average of 275 times each day by meetings, emails, or chats. The article argues that minor interruptions become more significant when they accumulate across hundreds or thousands of employees.

Technology friction also creates a “double toll” because employees lose working time while IT teams must spend capacity resolving issues such as recurring device problems, access requests, and troubleshooting sessions. The article recommends proactive management practices including integrated management, identity, and security tools; real-time device-health visibility; automated patching and configuration; and self-service workflows. It also presents Digital Employee Experience (DEX) as a way to measure employees’ interactions with devices, applications, and services so IT can identify recurring patterns and address gaps between employees and technology.

  • The article frames technology friction as a “double toll”: a single device or access problem reduces an employee’s working time while also consuming IT support capacity.
  • Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index is cited as finding employees are interrupted 275 times per day, or about once every two minutes during core work hours, illustrating how seemingly minor interruptions can become a workforce-wide productivity issue.
  • Digital Employee Experience (DEX) complements technical management by measuring the employee’s experience with devices, applications, and services, helping connect individual frustrations to recurring operational patterns.
  • Self-service workflows are presented as a way to reduce routine IT demand by enabling employees to handle simple needs, such as password resets or software installations, without waiting for support.

The article explains that small everyday technology problems, such as slow devices, login trouble, missing app access, and disruptive updates, can add up to major lost time across a company. Employees lose time trying to work, while IT staff also lose time fixing the same problems, especially in growing organizations with many Apple devices and small support teams. Watching for repeated issues and automating simple tasks can help companies prevent problems instead of waiting for employees to report them.

This is an evergreen best-practice and productivity perspective rather than coverage of a specific security incident, vulnerability, or urgent patch. It offers general guidance on proactive IT management and digital employee experience.

Optional · 25 announcement 21 Sep 2026 18:22 UTC · gpt-5.6-terra

Healthcare is Under Attack: Make Identity the Perimeter

Health-ISAC promotes a Radiant Logic webinar arguing that healthcare organizations should treat identity as their security perimeter, because weak access controls, excessive privileges, and lateral movement enable ransomware. The session focuses on reducing reliance on EDR and SIEM alone through stronger identity and access management practices.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Healthcare organizations are heavily targeted, according to the article’s discussion of real-world red-teaming experience.
  • 02The article says attackers often rely on weak identity controls, excessive privileges, and movement between systems rather than rare zero-day exploits.
  • 03It states that ransomware can be enabled by attackers moving through an organization after gaining access.
  • 04The article argues that relying too heavily on endpoint detection and response and security information and event management tools leaves a major defensive gap.
  • 05Health-ISAC promotes a recorded Radiant Logic webinar and registration for a second webinar session on identity-focused healthcare security.

Health-ISAC highlights a Radiant Logic webinar on why healthcare organizations are heavily targeted and why identity should be treated as the security perimeter. The presentation draws on Paul Dant’s real-world red-teaming experience. It states that attackers do not need rare zero-day exploits to gain access.

The article identifies weak identity controls, excessive privileges, and attackers moving between systems as drivers of ransomware. It argues that relying too heavily on endpoint detection and response and security information and event management tools leaves a major gap in defense. Readers can watch the recorded first webinar and register for a second session focused on what it takes to address these issues.

  • The article’s central recommendation is to treat identity controls—the rules governing who can access systems and what they can do—as the main security boundary for healthcare organizations.
  • It emphasizes that attackers do not necessarily need rare, previously unknown software flaws to compromise healthcare environments, because weak account controls and overly broad access can be sufficient.
  • The article highlights a defensive gap in relying primarily on tools that monitor endpoints and security logs, rather than preventing improper access and movement through systems.

The article promotes a Radiant Logic webinar about why healthcare organizations are frequent targets for criminals. It says attackers can get in through weak controls over user accounts, give themselves more access than they should have, and move through an organization’s systems, which can lead to ransomware that locks up data and systems. The broader message is that hospitals and other healthcare providers need to make sure each person has only the access they need, rather than relying mainly on tools that detect suspicious activity after it occurs.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a webinar promotion presenting general identity-security best practices for healthcare rather than reporting a specific incident, vulnerability, or urgent defensive action. Its discussion of excessive privilege and lateral movement is relevant but evergreen.
